item.title: More Functions in Math
item.description:
Functions — Beyond the Basics#

From mathematical functions to programming functions#

1. Where We Are#

We already know that a function:

  • Takes some input
  • Applies a rule
  • Produces an output
  • Has a domain and a range

For example:

f(x) = 2x + 3

If we give it 5:

f(5) = 2(5) + 3
 = 13

So far, we have mostly treated functions as rules for transforming values.

Now we will ask:

item.title: Functions in Math
item.description:
Functions — A Little Bit of Function#

1. What Is a Function?#

A function is a rule that takes an input and produces an output.

For example:

f(x) = 2x + 3

Give it 5:

f(5) = 2(5) + 3
 = 13

So we can think of a function as:

input → function → output

2. Evaluating Functions#

If:

f(x) = x² + 1

then:

f(2) = 2² + 1
 = 5

The x is simply replaced by the input.

item.title: Logic
item.description:
Logic: The Machinery of Reasoning#

You already know more logic than you think.

Every time you say:

“If it is raining, I should carry an umbrella.”

or:

“I will have tea if there is milk and sugar.”

or:

“I will go out if it is Saturday or Sunday.”

you are using logic.

You don’t need a computer, a formula, or a mathematics degree to use it. Logic is simply a way of describing how statements combine and how we reason from one statement to another.

item.title: The Missing Diamond
item.description:
🔎 The Missing Diamond#

The Case#

At 8:00 PM, the famous Blue Star Diamond disappeared from a locked display room at the City Museum.

There were only three people inside the museum at the time:

  • Arun — Security Guard

  • Meera — Museum Assistant

  • Ravi — Electrician

The police arrived immediately.

The display room had no broken windows or damaged locks.

🕵️ Clue 1 — The Security Camera#

The camera showed that the display room was opened at 7:42 PM.

item.title: Pirate Treasure
item.description:
The Pirate’s Treasure Map#

A Message from an Old Pirate#

A long time ago, a pirate buried a treasure somewhere on a distant island.

Before disappearing, he left behind a strange map.

It does not show mountains, rivers, or paths. Instead, it contains rows of numbers. The pirate claimed that anyone clever enough to follow the map would eventually discover the coordinates of his treasure.

Unfortunately, the map is written in a peculiar code.

item.title: Counting
item.description:
Counting, Numbers, and More#

Quiz#

We started the session with this quiz on an earlier topic.

Counting#

We explored the basics of counting, starting with a simple question: what is a digit?

We then considered how many numbers can be represented using ten fingers. This led to a thought experiment: if a crow with six fingers joined the count, how many numbers could we represent?

From there, the discussion introduced the idea of placeholder counting and how a count can be represented using binary.

item.title: Encryption/Decryption
item.description:
Ecnryption, Decryption, History…#

Puzzle#

Decrypt this puzzle. The clue is “12”. The other clue is “5”. It is important to consider both shapes and colors together.

Puzzle Image#

History#

  • Why this activity?
  • A brief history of computing
  • Entscheidungsproblem by David Hilbert
  • Kurt Gödel publishes his incompleteness theorems
  • Inspired by all this Alan Turing proves that a general solution to Hilbert’s question is impossible and proceeds to find a limit to what can be computed. In doing so he invents the Turing Machine which is what modern computers are primarily based on.
  • Turing gets enlisted by the British government to work in Bletchley Park on the Engima project
  • Germans use the Engima machine to encrypt messages and send to their troops. This proves very hard to crack
  • With some luck and ingenuity - and the clever use of a computer - Alan Turing solves this problem, thus setting off the modern computer age.
